title: Impacts of Dynamic LED Lighting on the Well-Being and Experience of Office Occupants
research_question: To better understand the impact of dynamic LED lighting with daily variation in illuminance and CCT levels on office occupants' health, well-being, and experience, specifically investigating if it reduces stress, maintains productivity, improves alertness, sleep quality, mood, satisfaction, visual comfort, and perceived light naturalness.

participants.description: 15 participants (9 male, mean age 38) from various work units at a large midwestern medical institution. Predominantly white and middle class. Mostly moderate morning and intermediate chronotypes. Baseline perceived sleep quality slightly worse (PSQI > 5).
participants.recruitment: Recruited across various work units at a large midwestern medical institution. Underwent a screening process including medical chart review, OTC medication assessment, and travel history. Gave written informed consent.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four lighting conditions in three combined office modules (124 m² open office) in a living lab. Conditions included two static and two dynamic profiles, mimicking Japanese (JP) and US office settings. Dynamic profiles varied illuminance and CCT throughout the day, increasing in the morning and decreasing in the afternoon to mimic natural daylight. JP conditions had higher illuminance (500-700 lux) and CCT (3500-6000 K) than US conditions (300-500 lux, 3000-5000 K).

measures.construct: Physiological stress (skin conductance level, NS-SCR amplitudes, phasic driver)
measures.instrument: Empatica E4 (EDA, photoplethysmograph, 3-axis accelerometer, skin temperature)

measures.construct: Objective sleep parameters (total sleep time, sleep onset, deep sleep time, light sleep time, sleep onset latency, sleep midpoint, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, REM sleep time)
Perceived daily productivity, satisfaction with environment, environment impact on productivity
Satisfaction with lighting conditions, other environmental conditions, overall environment
Visual comfort (eye fatigue, blurred vision, headache)
measures.instrument: Headache and Eye Strain Scale (H and ES)
Positive Affect Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) survey (5-point Likert scale)

mechanisms: Differences in illuminance and CCT levels between country-specific conditions may explain dichotomous mood effects.
Bright light is known to improve affect and reduce distress, supporting observed mood benefits.
Lack of difference in negative affect may explain no significant difference in stress levels.
Decrease in deep sleep time may lead to less restorative sleep, impacting perceived sleep quality.
Dynamic lighting control profiles may need optimization to generate stronger non-visual effects.
The spectral power distribution (SPD) peak at 450 nm in the blue range might not be the most sensitive for circadian stimulus (460-480 nm range suggested by other studies).
Insufficient blue light dosage or duration in the morning may not be enough to entrain circadian rhythm effectively.
Participants may perceive their environment holistically, leading to perceived improvements in other environmental factors (e.g., acoustic, air movement) when lighting conditions change.
moderators: week number (for perceived sleep quality in JP-D condition)
country-specific conditions (US vs. JP, implicitly moderating mood and sleep outcomes)
implementation_implications: Dynamic lighting can be an effective solution to reduce daytime sleepiness in offices.
Future lighting systems should aim for peak spectral power at 460–480 nm to enhance physiological and behavioral effects.
Dynamic lighting profiles could be revised to increase morning illuminance/CCT levels and/or postpone afternoon decreases to better entrain human circadian systems.
Optimized levels of illuminance, CCT, and peak blue light spectrum in morning vs. afternoon are key for circadian entrainment.
Longer study periods with more lighting conditions are needed to separate the contributions of illuminance and CCT.
Continuous eye-level lighting monitoring and after-office-hour behavior/sleep tracking could provide further insights into dynamic lighting effectiveness in offices and homes.

limitations: The study design did not allow for systematic isolation of the individual impacts of illuminance versus CCT.

The dynamic lighting control profile may need further optimization to generate stronger non-visual effects, as the blue light SPD peak (450 nm) might not be optimal for circadian stimulus (460-480 nm).

Participants' exposure to bright-blue light in the morning might have been insufficient to effectively entrain their circadian rhythm (total blue light dosage difference between dynamic and static conditions was not significant enough).
No measurements of participants' lighting exposure after office hours were collected due to lack of mature tools for continuous eye-level monitoring.
A longer test period with more lighting conditions is recommended to unambiguously separate the contributions of illuminance and CCT.

paper_metadata.crossref_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: As a critical factor in the built environment, lighting presents considerable influence on occupants. Previous research across static lighting conditions has found that both illuminance and correlated color temperature (CCT) affect occupants’ physiological and psychological functioning. However, little research has been conducted on the non-visual impacts of dynamic lighting with daily variation in illuminance and CCT levels. The purpose of this study is to better understand the impact of dynamic lighting on office occupants’ health, well-being and experience at a living lab. Fifteen participants were recruited to work in three office modules for four months. Four lighting conditions were designed and implemented in this study, including two static lighting conditions and two dynamic lighting conditions with a specific predefined control scheme. A prototype lighting system with enhanced control capabilities was configured and implemented to ensure the desired lighting environment protocol. Both objective methods and subjective surveys were used to assess the behavioral and physiological outcomes of interest, including mental stress, sleep, productivity, satisfaction, mood, visual comfort and perceived naturalness. The results showed that the daytime behavioral impacts were either positive or mixed. Specifically, a significant alertness increase was observed in the afternoon, indicating a potential solution to reduce the natural feelings of sleepiness during the workday. There was also a marginal benefit for mood. The nighttime impacts include a significant decrease in perceived sleep quality and sleep time after subjects were exposed to dynamic lighting. No significant differences were observed for mental stress, productivity, visual comfort, or perceived naturalness. The findings present additional insights into the non-visual impacts of dynamic lighting and give recommendations for further investigations.
